history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a proposed scientific study by Harvard University aimed at investigating the behavior of aerosol particles in the stratosphere. Led by principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators, including David Keith, the concept was presented publicly, notably at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. This experiment was designed to enhance computer models assessing the risks and benefits of solar geoengineering, specifically solar radiation management, but it was not intended as a deployment of geoengineering or a method to cool the planet. The proposed experiment involved a balloon gondola operating at approximately 20 km altitude, releasing about 100 grams to less than 2 kilograms of calcium carbonate into a defined volume for measurement of aerosol microphysics and light scattering. A planned platform test in Sweden in 2021 was limited to hardware evaluation and was suspended by the SCoPEx Advisory Committee pending societal engagement, with no materials released. In March 2024, Harvard announced that Keutsch would not continue with SCoPEx, and the platform is expected to be repurposed for other stratospheric research.

Its central aim is to hold the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5°C. Parties submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) describing their mitigation plans; the Agreement uses a ratchet mechanism of successive NDCs rather than a single top-down allocation of tonnes. The United States joined, withdrew under the first Trump administration, and rejoined under the Biden administration; participation has been politically contested but the scientific case for rapid emissions cuts is independent of any one administration. Meeting Paris temperature goals requires deep, sustained cuts in fossil CO2, methane and other greenhouse gases, plus protection of carbon sinks — not covert aviation spraying.
